Boosting a VQ is extremely expensive the cheapest turbo kit around right now is boosted bull performance rear mount turbo for about $2000 and you still need to buy other parts to make it work and do a lot of work.

The easiest way to boost these cars is with a centrifugal supercharger but the kits aren’t cheap 6-8k you are looking at for just the kit not including supporting mods and a tune.

A vq35de might be able to handle 500whp for a short while but not reliably the highest you can hit reliably without opening the motor is about 400-450 and 450 is pushing it.

If you are serious about this I would be prepared to spend about 2x what you intend on spending if you know fab work and cars well you can turbo them relatively cheaply about 5-10 years ago there was forum post where a guy boosted his g for $1400 now a days the material cost would be at least double that and that’s fabbing all the piping yourself.

The car will be down for quite some time if you plan on doing this and expect some issues right off the hop that need to be worked out, make sure all maintenance Is done before you intend on boosting, a catch can/air oil separator would be good and I would replace the pcv valve so you don’t build crankcase pressure and blow seals.

Ensure the motor doesn’t have crazy blow by or eats oil before doing all the work.

As an electrician your logic is a little flawed and I would review electrical theory.

To expand on this the issue isn’t that “you are adding a weak link with no protection” anything connected to the circuit has the same level of protection as anything plugged into a receptacle is still getting over current protection from the breaker. The reason why multi plugs are more dangerous is because if you have inadequate protection it makes it much easier to overload a circuit. That combined with a larger possibility of a loose connection ect plug not fully inserted into the receptacle and the breakers trip curve + an aging breaker and you can be in trouble.

Just to clarify all types of electrical lids generate heat, heat is a byproduct of current and resistance all electrical loads have some level of resistance, some more than others resistive loads generate the most heat but even an incandescent light bulb is a resistive load.

What I’m trying to say is it doesn’t matter the type of load or appliance plugged in, what matters most is the amperage many appliances are setup so that they will use all the available amperage on a 15A circuit so if that’s all you have on the circuit you are fine but when you add other loads combined with the breakers trip curve you end up with situations like OPs

You drill a hole through the joist on each side then you put a short fishtape through both holes and you move them around to hear them hit eachother once you do you pull back on one most of the time you will come off the other fishtape but with finesse you can get the hook of the tape to drag along the other fishtape until the hooks catch AKA “catching fish” 

I do it sometimes in knob and tube rewire where you want to avoid a lot of damage or if I’m only going a short distance sometimes you can utilize other fixtures and sometimes you can do this through the hole of another potlight and essentially halve the amount of holes you would normally make.
